distr::GaussianMixture¶

A mixture of normal distributions: the density is a weighted sum of normal densities, which builds multimodal and skewed shapes from simple parts.

Signature¶

distr::GaussianMixture(const pluss::Series& weights, const pluss::Series& means, const pluss::Series& stddevs);
pluss::Series distr::GaussianMixture::pdf(const pluss::Series& x) const;
pluss::Series distr::GaussianMixture::cdf(const pluss::Series& x) const;
pluss::Series distr::GaussianMixture::sample(std::initializer_list<std::int64_t> sizes, pluss::Config cfg = {}, std::uint64_t seed = 0) const;
pluss::Series distr::GaussianMixture::cumulant(std::int64_t order) const;
distr::GaussianMixtureFit distr::GaussianMixture::MLE(const pluss::Series& x) const;

What It Does¶

A Gaussian mixture is the distribution of a variable drawn in two steps: first one of k components is chosen with probability weights[j], then the value is drawn from the normal distribution N(means[j], stddevs[j]²). The density is sum_j weights[j] N(x; means[j], stddevs[j]²). Mixtures model populations that are really several groups (heights of a mixed sample, returns in calm and turbulent markets), and they approximate almost any smooth density as the number of components grows.

MLE fits the weights, means and standard deviations by the expectation-maximisation algorithm, starting from the values stored in the object (their number is the number of components). It alternates between computing, for each observation, the probability that each component produced it, and re-estimating each component from the observations weighted by those probabilities, and stops when the log-likelihood no longer changes. Different starting values reach the same maximum unless the likelihood has several local maxima, so for a real problem try a few starts and keep the highest log-likelihood.

Support: all real numbers.

Parameters¶

const pluss::Series& weights

The component weights, positive and summing to one.

const pluss::Series& means

The component means, one per weight.

const pluss::Series& stddevs

The component standard deviations, positive, one per weight.

const pluss::Series& x

The points at which to evaluate, or (for MLE) the observed values to fit.

std::initializer_list<std::int64_t> sizes

The shape of the array of random draws.

pluss::Config cfg

The dtype and platform of the draws; the default is Float32 on the CPU.

std::uint64_t seed

The seed of the stream; the same seed gives the same draws.

std::int64_t order

The order of the cumulant: 1 is the mean and 2 the variance of the mixture.

Returns¶

pdf and cdf return a Series of the shape of x; sample a Series of the requested shape; MLE a GaussianMixtureFit with the fields weights, means and stddevs and the methods of a fit (loglik, stderr, confint, vcov, score, observed_inf).

Errors¶

  • Weights that are not positive, do not sum to one, or have a different length from the means and standard deviations are refused.

  • Non-positive standard deviations are refused.

Practical Examples¶

Example 1¶

Example 1 builds a two-component mixture and evaluates its density and distribution function. The mixture is bimodal: the density has a tall narrow peak near -2 (30% of the mass) and a lower, wider one near 1.5 (70%).

#include <pluss/ma.h>
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

namespace distr = pluss::subsp::stats::distr;

int main() {
  const auto f64 = pluss::Config{}.with_dtype(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(4);

  const distr::GaussianMixture mixture{pluss::make_series({0.3, 0.7}, f64), pluss::make_series({-2.0, 1.5}, f64), pluss::make_series({0.8, 1.2}, f64)};
  const auto x = pluss::make_series({-4.0, -2.0, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5, 4.0}, f64);

  std::cout << "x:";
  for (double v : x.host<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "pdf:";
  for (double v : mixture.pdf(x).host<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "cdf:";
  for (double v : mixture.cdf(x).host<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "cumulant(1), the mean: " << mixture.cumulant(1).item<double>() << '\n';
  std::cout << "cumulant(2), the variance: " << mixture.cumulant(2).item<double>() << '\n';
}

Output

x: -4.0000 -2.0000 -0.5000 0.5000 1.5000 4.0000
pdf: 0.0066 0.1529 0.0838 0.1656 0.2327 0.0266
cdf: 0.0019 0.1512 0.3243 0.4414 0.6500 0.9870
cumulant(1), the mean: 0.4500
cumulant(2), the variance: 3.7725

The density is largest on this grid at x = 1.5 (0.2327), in the wider, heavier component, and the distribution function runs from 0.0019 at x = -4 to 0.987 at x = 4. cumulant(1) is 0.45, the weighted mean of the component means (0.3 × -2 + 0.7 × 1.5), and cumulant(2) is the variance of the whole mixture, 3.7725: larger than either component’s variance because the two centres are far apart.

Example 2¶

Example 2 checks the mixture against its definition: the density is the weighted sum of the two normal densities, and the mean is the weighted sum of the component means.

#include <pluss/ma.h>
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

namespace distr = pluss::subsp::stats::distr;

int main() {
  const auto f64 = pluss::Config{}.with_dtype(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(6);

  const distr::GaussianMixture mixture{pluss::make_series({0.3, 0.7}, f64), pluss::make_series({-2.0, 1.5}, f64), pluss::make_series({0.8, 1.2}, f64)};
  const auto x = pluss::make_series({-4.0, -2.0, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5, 4.0}, f64);

  const auto by_hand = distr::Normal{-2.0, 0.8}.pdf(x) * 0.3 + distr::Normal{1.5, 1.2}.pdf(x) * 0.7;
  std::cout << "mixture pdf:";
  for (double v : mixture.pdf(x).host<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "weighted sum:";
  for (double v : by_hand.host<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << std::scientific << std::setprecision(2) << "largest difference: " << (mixture.pdf(x) - by_hand).abs().max().item<double>() << '\n';
  std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(6) << "weighted mean of the components: " << 0.3 * -2.0 + 0.7 * 1.5 << "   cumulant(1): " << mixture.cumulant(1).item<double>() << '\n';
}

Output

mixture pdf: 0.006579 0.152911 0.083823 0.165582 0.232727 0.026567
weighted sum: 0.006579 0.152911 0.083823 0.165582 0.232727 0.026567
largest difference: 0.00e+00
weighted mean of the components: 0.450000   cumulant(1): 0.450000

The mixture density equals the weighted sum of the two normal densities at every point (largest difference 0, to the printed digits), and cumulant(1) equals the weighted mean of the component means, 0.45.

Example 3¶

Example 3 fits the mixture back to 600 draws by the expectation-maximisation algorithm from two very different starting points, which reach the same fit, and reads the standard errors and a confidence interval.

#include <pluss/ma.h>
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

namespace distr = pluss::subsp::stats::distr;

int main() {
  const auto f64 = pluss::Config{}.with_dtype(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(4);

  const distr::GaussianMixture truth{pluss::make_series({0.3, 0.7}, f64), pluss::make_series({-2.0, 1.5}, f64), pluss::make_series({0.8, 1.2}, f64)};
  const auto x = truth.sample({600}, f64, 77ULL);

  for (const std::vector<double> start : {std::vector<double>{-1.0, 1.0}, std::vector<double>{-3.0, 3.0}}) {
    const auto fit = distr::GaussianMixture{pluss::make_series({0.5, 0.5}, f64), pluss::make_series(start, f64), pluss::make_series({1.0, 1.0}, f64)}.MLE(x);
    std::cout << "start at the means: " << start[0] << ' ' << start[1] << '\n';
    std::cout << "  weights:";
    for (double v : fit.weights.host<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
    std::cout << '\n';
    std::cout << "  means:";
    for (double v : fit.means.host<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
    std::cout << '\n';
    std::cout << "  stddevs:";
    for (double v : fit.stddevs.host<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
    std::cout << '\n';
    std::cout << "  loglik: " << fit.loglik(x).item<double>() << '\n';
  }
  const auto fit = distr::GaussianMixture{pluss::make_series({0.5, 0.5}, f64), pluss::make_series({-1.0, 1.0}, f64), pluss::make_series({1.0, 1.0}, f64)}.MLE(x);
  std::cout << "stderr of (w1, w2, m1, m2, s1, s2):";
  for (double v : fit.stderr(x).host<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
}

Output

start at the means: -1.0000 1.0000
  weights: 0.2797 0.7203
  means: -2.0551 1.4474
  stddevs: 0.8873 1.2661
  loglik: -1211.7021
start at the means: -3.0000 3.0000
  weights: 0.2797 0.7203
  means: -2.0551 1.4474
  stddevs: 0.8873 1.2661
  loglik: -1211.7021
stderr of (w1, w2, m1, m2, s1, s2): 0.0451 0.0451 0.2089 0.1389 0.1354 0.0945

Both starting points reach the same fit: weights 0.2797 and 0.7203, means -2.0551 and 1.4474, standard deviations 0.8873 and 1.2661, log-likelihood -1211.70, against the generating values 0.3 and 0.7, -2 and 1.5, 0.8 and 1.2. The standard errors, in the order (w1, w2, m1, m2, s1, s2), show the two weights are tied (0.0451 each, since they sum to one) and that the mean of the narrow component (0.2089) is the least precise: it rests on fewer observations.

Example 4¶

Example 4 turns the fitted mixture into a classifier. By Bayes’ rule the probability that an observation came from the first component is w1 N(x; m1, s1²) divided by the mixture density, computed from the fitted parameters alone.

#include <pluss/ma.h>
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

namespace distr = pluss::subsp::stats::distr;

int main() {
  const auto f64 = pluss::Config{}.with_dtype(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(3);

  const distr::GaussianMixture truth{pluss::make_series({0.3, 0.7}, f64), pluss::make_series({-2.0, 1.5}, f64), pluss::make_series({0.8, 1.2}, f64)};
  const auto fit = distr::GaussianMixture{pluss::make_series({0.5, 0.5}, f64), pluss::make_series({-1.0, 1.0}, f64), pluss::make_series({1.0, 1.0}, f64)}.MLE(truth.sample({600}, f64, 77ULL));

  const auto w = fit.weights.host<double>(), m = fit.means.host<double>(), s = fit.stddevs.host<double>();
  const auto x = pluss::make_series({-3.0, -1.5, -0.5, 0.0, 0.5, 1.5}, f64);
  const auto first = distr::Normal{m[0], s[0]}.pdf(x) * w[0];
  const auto second = distr::Normal{m[1], s[1]}.pdf(x) * w[1];

  std::cout << "x:";
  for (double v : x.host<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "P(first component | x):";
  for (double v : (first / (first + second)).host<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
}

Output

x: -3.000 -1.500 -0.500 0.000 0.500 1.500
P(first component | x): 0.993 0.873 0.280 0.068 0.011 0.000

The probability of the first component falls from 0.993 at x = -3 to 0.873 at -1.5 and 0.280 at -0.5, passes one half near x = -1, and is essentially zero from 0.5 on: a point is assigned to the narrow component only on the left, where the wide component has little mass.
